messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 71
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Nanny
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Location: Going to or near the place where the event happened, People Pleasing: go along with whatever others want to feel safe, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Negative Appraisals: Inadequacy: I am inadequate, No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Leila was a 71-year-old Middle Eastern woman who had spent much of her adult life in the United States, where she worked as a nanny and kept herself busy with the routines of other people’s children, meals, and school schedules. She lived with her husband, and until the event that brought her to treatment, she had described herself as steady, careful, and used to making herself useful. That changed on an afternoon when she witnessed a violent incident near a place she had reason to be. She did not describe it as something that happened to her directly, but she was there, close enough to see the fear, the confusion, and the helplessness unfold in front of her. What stayed with her was not a single image alone but the sequence of it: the suddenness, the other people’s reaction, and the sense that she had been standing in the middle of something dangerous without being able to stop it. In the days afterward, she found that the area where it happened no longer felt like an ordinary part of the city. Even the thought of going back there made her tighten up, and over time she began to avoid that location and anywhere near it, taking longer routes and rearranging errands so she would not have to pass close by.

For a while, Leila tried to keep going as before, and in some ways she became even more accommodating. In her work as a nanny, she said she found herself agreeing quickly to whatever the parents wanted, even when it made her uncomfortable, because it felt safer not to disagree. At home and in the community, she did the same, letting others choose the restaurant, the route, the timing, and the plan. She had come to believe that if she stayed agreeable, stayed quiet, and did not draw attention to herself, she could reduce the chance of something bad happening. Alongside that, she worked hard not to think about the event. When the memory came into her mind, she pushed it away immediately, telling herself to stop, to focus on the present task, to keep busy with the child she was caring for or the items she needed at the store. She preferred not to linger on any detail, because once she let herself think about it, the scene seemed to rise up with a force that made it hard to settle again.

As the weeks turned into months, Leila became increasingly watchful in the everyday world. She noticed faces, hands, and body movements with an intensity that other people did not seem to share. When she was out walking or standing in line, she found herself watching other people closely for signs that they might harm her. She frequently looked behind her, even on familiar streets, checking to see if someone was following. In public places she kept herself on alert, scanning doorways and corners, readying herself before she could explain exactly what she expected. These habits followed her into her workday. Caring for young children required her to go out to parks, sidewalks, and neighborhood streets, and she did so while staying noticeably on guard, less able to relax into the ordinary rhythm of the job. She did not say she was afraid of the children or of the parents, but she was always alert to the larger world around them, as though danger might appear without warning.

Leila also spoke with a painful sense of failure that had settled into her view of herself. She believed she should have protected others and failed. She replayed the scene in her mind not as an opportunity to act but as a measure of what she had not done, and that thought sat heavily on her. Alongside that was her conviction that the people responsible had faced no consequences. The lack of accountability troubled her deeply; it left the event feeling unfinished, unresolved, and unfair in a way she could not put down. She also used blunt words about herself, saying, in essence, that she was inadequate. It was not a passing mood but a judgment she had started to carry into how she saw her own worth, as if her inability to prevent what she had witnessed had exposed something fundamentally lacking in her.

By the time she sought help, Leila was tired of living around the memory and its aftermath. She was no longer satisfied with simply arranging her days to avoid the place where the event happened, or with constantly yielding to others so she could feel safe. The vigilance had become exhausting, and she was worried by how much effort it took to move through ordinary life without scanning, checking, and bracing herself. What brought her in was the growing sense that she could not keep managing this alone, especially as it began to affect the ease and confidence she needed in her work and in daily routines. What she feared most was being caught unprepared in another dangerous moment; what she hoped for was some way to live without feeling that she had to keep herself hidden, watchful, and forever responsible for what she had not been able to prevent.
